title: Utilities shift large-load risk onto customers via new tariff terms
plain: Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory finds a sharp increase since early 2025 in the number of active and proposed utility tariffs specifically targeting large loads, chiefly data centers. These tariffs increasingly incorporate upfront payments, exit fees, and multi-year ramp schedules that phase in deman

angles.claim: AI teams planning new training or inference clusters must now budget for exit fees and multi-year ramp schedules as standard interconnection costs, not contingencies.
angles.audience: AI infrastructure and capacity planning leads at data-center operators and their utility counterparts
angles.rank_reason: Directly changes a capital planning and site-selection decision an AI engineering leader must make before committing to a build.

angles.claim: Rising qualifying-demand thresholds mean some AI compute buildouts that once triggered large-load review will now fall outside it, and teams should recheck which tariff regime applies.
angles.audience: AI infrastructure leads and utility rates counterparts negotiating power for compute buildouts
angles.rank_reason: Reaches the reader and prompts a concrete check, though it is narrower than the first angle since it only affects classification, not total exposure.

angles.claim: Utilities are converting stranded-asset risk from cancelled or under-delivered AI projects into contractual minimum-take obligations that AI teams must model into worst-case shutdown costs.
angles.audience: AI engineering and finance leads sizing exit risk on committed compute projects
angles.rank_reason: Ranks last because it restates the source's framing of risk-shifting with less new decision content than the first two angles.
